text: Your vital lung capacity falls by roughly 200 ml each decade from your twenties on — by 70, most people are down to about 75% of what they had at 30. Posture affects how well you use what's left: in a small study of healthy young men, simply holding a forward-head position measurably reduced inspiratory muscle strength. Keeping your ribcage and upper back mobile supports the mechanics of a full breath — though no study has yet shown it slows the age-related decline itself.
source: Wang et al., Frontiers in Immunology, 2024 (ageing-lung review); Zafar et al., BioMed Research International, 2018 (n=15)

text: About 28-35% of adults over 65 fall each year, rising to 32-42% for those over 70. Falls are the leading cause of injury death in older adults, and many are preventable. Stretching reliably improves joint range of motion, and one small trial found hip and ankle stretching improved walking speed in older adults. The strongest fall-prevention evidence, though, is for balance and strength training — so use stretching alongside those, not instead of them.
source: WHO, Global Report on Falls Prevention in Older Age, 2007; Sadaqa et al., Frontiers in Public Health, 2023; Christiansen, Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, 2008 (n=37)

text: Kyphosis — that rounded upper back — isn't only cosmetic. It's associated with reduced lung function and poorer balance, though that evidence is observational. One study of older adults found about 40% higher mortality in those with hyperkyphotic posture; a later study measuring the curve on X-ray didn't confirm it, so treat it as a signal rather than a settled risk. Spine-strengthening and posture training do reduce the curve — by about 3 degrees over six months in the best trial — so think of it as slowing a drift, not reversing one.
source: Kado et al., Journal of the American Geriatrics Society, 2004; Cours et al., Journal of the American Geriatrics Society, 2023; Katzman et al., Osteoporosis International, 2017

text: Adults are sedentary for 10 or more hours a day, and office workers spend roughly three-quarters of their working hours sitting. People who sit more than seven hours a day average about 6 degrees less hip extension than people who sit little — an association, not proof that sitting caused it. The encouraging part: consistent stretching reliably improves that range, and much of the gain comes from your nervous system raising its tolerance rather than from tissue permanently lengthening.
source: Boukabache et al., Musculoskeletal Science and Practice, 2021; Diaz et al., Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017; Parry & Straker, BMC Public Health, 2013

text: Muscle stiffness isn't only about the muscle — much of it is your nervous system. Reviewing the stretching literature, researchers found that the gains from a single session, or from a 3-to-8-week program, come mostly from increased tolerance to the stretch sensation rather than from tissue permanently lengthening. Whether longer programs change the tissue itself hasn't yet been tested.
source: Weppler & Magnusson, Physical Therapy, 2010

text: Balance isn't a talent — it's a skill that fades without practice. Among adults aged 51 to 75, those who couldn't hold a 10-second one-legged stance had about 1.8 times the risk of dying over the next seven years, even after accounting for age, sex, BMI and existing illness. That's an association, not a sentence — and balance responds well to training. Just budget real practice: the trials that move the needle add up to hours, not seconds a day.
source: Araujo et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2022; Chen et al., PLoS One, 2026 (dose-response meta-analysis)

text: Grip strength predicts all-cause mortality better than systolic blood pressure. Every 5-kilogram decrease in grip strength is associated with a 16% higher risk of death from any cause. It's not that squeezing a hand towel makes you live longer on its own — grip is a window into whole-body strength, and strength is the window into how well you age.
source: Leong et al., The Lancet, 2015 (PURE study, 139,691 adults across 17 countries)

text: Getting down to the floor and back up without your hands tests leg strength, flexibility and balance at once. In a study of 2,002 Brazilian adults aged 51 to 80, each extra point on a 10-point sit-and-rise score went with about 21% better survival over roughly six years, and the lowest scorers had about five times the mortality of the highest. The study adjusted only for age, sex and body weight, so read a low score as a sign of overall fitness, not a verdict.
source: Brito et al., European Journal of Preventive Cardiology, 2014 (retrospective cohort, n=2,002)

text: Complex movement patterns — ones that coordinate many joints and muscle groups — are associated with better-preserved thinking in older adults. They aren't the only route: in a year-long trial of adults aged 62 to 79, coordination training and brisk walking each improved attention compared with a control group, apparently through different brain networks. It was a small trial with many dropouts, so read it as encouraging rather than settled.
source: Voelcker-Rehage & Niemann, Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, 2013; Voelcker-Rehage, Godde & Staudinger, Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 2011

text: Frozen shoulder — adhesive capsulitis — affects about 2 to 5% of people. People with diabetes are around five times more likely to develop it, and thyroid disease raises the risk too. It usually improves over one to two years, though some people are left with stiffness that lasts. Its cause is unknown, so no exercise has been shown to prevent it.
source: Ramirez, American Family Physician, 2019

text: Low back pain is the world's leading cause of years lived with disability, and most adults will have it at some point — though lifetime estimates vary widely between studies, from about 11% to 84%. For acute back pain, Cochrane evidence shows staying active gives a small advantage over bed rest, with no difference for sciatica, and guidelines no longer recommend prolonged bed rest.
source: GBD 2019 Diseases and Injuries Collaborators, Lancet, 2020; Walker, Journal of Spinal Disorders, 2000; Dahm et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2010

text: In a study of more than 3,000 adults aged 70 to 79, those with the weakest thigh (knee-extensor) strength were about twice as likely to develop difficulty walking or climbing stairs over the next two and a half years as the strongest. Rising from a chair without your hands is a practical way to keep working those muscles — though no study has set a daily number.
source: Visser et al., Journals of Gerontology: Series A, 2005 (Health ABC, n=3,075)

text: Your upper back is built to rotate and extend, and sitting appears to cost some of that: in 92 young adults, those sitting more than seven hours a day had about 14% less thoracic rotation than physically active peers (65 degrees versus 75). The study was observational and in 18-to-30-year-olds, so it can't tell us about cause or about decline later in life.
source: Heneghan et al., BMJ Open, 2018 (n=92)

text: Your calf muscles act as a 'second heart', squeezing the leg veins to push blood back toward the chest when you walk. In a randomised trial of people with chronic venous insufficiency, a structured calf-strengthening program measurably improved that pump after six months, though it didn't change symptom scores. Cochrane rates the overall evidence for exercise in venous insufficiency as very low quality, so treat calf work as sensible rather than proven.
source: Padberg et al., Journal of Vascular Surgery, 2004 (randomised, n=31); Araujo et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2016

text: Breathing at about six breaths a minute — far slower than most of us ever breathe — reliably raises heart rate variability, the standard marker of vagal, rest-and-digest activity. A 2022 review pooled 223 studies and found it during the session, straight after a single session, and after weeks of practice. What it does not reliably do is lower blood pressure; the largest pooled analysis of that found no effect.
source: Laborde et al., Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, 2022 (meta-analysis, 223 studies); de Freitas Gonçalves et al., Health Science Reports, 2022 (22 studies, 17,214 people)

text: Vagal traffic to the heart peaks on the out-breath — which is why your pulse quickens a little as you breathe in and settles as you breathe out, and why long exhales feel calming. How much the lengthening itself adds is unsettled: the best-designed trials found a one-to-two in-out ratio gave no more heart rate variability than an even one at the same slow rate. The slowing appears to do most of the work.
source: Farmer et al., Journal of Physiology, 2016 (brainstem mechanism, animal study); Meehan et al., Applied Psychophysiology and Biofeedback, 2024 (two randomised experiments); Bae et al., Psychophysiology, 2021

text: Five minutes a day of cyclic sighing — two inhales through the nose, then one long slow exhale — improved mood and slowed resting breathing more than five minutes of mindfulness meditation did, over a month, in a randomised study of 108 people. Treat it as promising rather than settled: small groups, four weeks, no follow-up, and the trial was registered after it began.
source: Balban et al., Cell Reports Medicine, 2023 (randomised, n=108, 4 weeks)

text: Nostril-regulated breathing does slow the heart: a 2026 meta-analysis of seven trials in 683 people with high blood pressure found a consistent drop in heart rate, though the blood-pressure effect did not survive the stricter statistical model. The evidence points at the slowness rather than the nostrils — compared head to head, left- and right-nostril practices produced the same changes, and the breathing rate fell either way.
source: Chidambaram et al., Indian Heart Journal, 2026 (7 RCTs, 683 people); Telles et al., International Journal of Yoga, 2024 (randomised crossover, n=47)

text: Breathing through the nose does something mouth-breathing does not: the airflow paces electrical rhythms in the brain's memory and emotion centres. Recordings made inside the brains of eight epilepsy patients found those rhythms tracking the breath — and fading when breathing was diverted to the mouth. It is the airflow itself that carries the signal, not extra oxygen.
source: Zelano et al., Journal of Neuroscience, 2016 (intracranial recordings, n=8; behavioural tasks, n=62 and n=33)

text: Pursed-lip breathing — in through the nose, out slowly through pursed lips — is a clinical technique for breathlessness rather than a relaxation fad. In COPD trials it reduces the trapped air that makes the next breath harder to take. Its effect on how far people can walk is inconsistent: in one crossover only about a quarter of patients improved, those with the weakest outward flow.
source: Cabral et al., European Journal of Physical and Rehabilitation Medicine, 2015 (randomised crossover, n=40); de Araujo et al., Journal of Rehabilitation Medicine, 2015 (n=25)

text: Eight weeks of daily diaphragmatic breathing lowered cortisol and improved sustained attention in forty healthy adults. Read it as a signal rather than a verdict: people were assigned by the order they registered rather than at random, and the comparison group did nothing at all, so expectation is uncontrolled. The direction matches the rest of this evidence — slow breathing shifts autonomic state.
source: Ma et al., Frontiers in Psychology, 2017 (n=40, quasi-randomised, no active control)

text: The 4-7-8 pattern is everywhere, but the specific counts have little behind them. In the one head-to-head test — 84 people, four breathing conditions — plain six-breaths-a-minute raised heart rate variability more than 4-7-8 did, and none of the patterns shifted mood. There is no published trial of it for sleep, its most common claim. The counts are a way to breathe slowly, not the active ingredient.
source: Marchant et al., Applied Psychophysiology and Biofeedback, 2025 (n=84); Vierra et al., Physiological Reports, 2022 (n=43, uncontrolled)

text: In a Cochrane review of 27 trials in adults with neck pain, moderate-quality evidence supported strength training for the neck, shoulder and shoulder-blade muscles to ease long-lasting neck pain, at least in the short term. Stretching on its own may not change pain (low-quality evidence). The authors found no high-quality evidence, so some uncertainty remains.
source: Gross et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2015 (27 RCTs, n=2,485)

text: A 2024 review pooled 8 trials of office workers with chronic neck pain. Strengthening the neck, shoulder and shoulder-blade muscles reduced neck pain and disability compared with control groups. The catch: all 8 trials had a high risk of bias, and the authors rate the certainty of the evidence as low.
source: Jones et al., Applied Ergonomics, 2024 (meta-analysis of 8 RCTs)

text: In the CSAW trial, 313 people with at least three months of shoulder pain — despite exercise therapy and a steroid injection — got decompression surgery, placebo keyhole surgery, or no treatment. At six months, real surgery did no better than the placebo. Both surgeries beat no treatment slightly, but not by a clinically important amount.
source: Beard et al., Lancet, 2018 (randomised placebo-controlled trial, n=313)

text: A Cochrane review of exercise for hand osteoarthritis found small improvements in hand pain, function and finger stiffness right after the programmes (pain pooled from 5 trials, 381 people). The authors rated the evidence low quality, questioned whether effects this small matter clinically, and found they were not sustained at later follow-up. It studied people with hand osteoarthritis, not all older adults.
source: Østerås et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2017 (systematic review of RCTs, n=381)

text: Exercise can ease hip osteoarthritis a little. A 2026 Cochrane review of 18 trials (1,368 people) found that, compared with no treatment or usual care, land-based exercise probably reduces pain and improves physical function slightly. The authors judged these average changes unlikely to be clinically meaningful, and noted most trials were small and unblinded.
source: Hall et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2026 (18 RCTs, n=1,368)

text: Your hip abductors are the muscles on the outside of your hip. An Australian study followed 952 adults aged 65 and over for a median of 11.5 years: those with stronger hip abductors were less likely to need emergency care after a fall. Hip flexor strength showed no such link. This is an association only — it does not prove that strengthening these muscles prevents falls.
source: Yosef et al., Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle, 2026 (prospective cohort, n=952)

text: A 2024 Cochrane review of 139 trials (12,468 people with knee osteoarthritis) found land-based exercise probably improves pain and physical function in the short term compared with control groups, and no single type of exercise stood out. The authors caution the benefits are of uncertain clinical importance, and most participants knew they were exercising, which may have contributed.
source: Lawford et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2024 (139 RCTs, n=12,468)

text: Strength can still be built very late in life. In a 10-week trial, 100 frail nursing-home residents (average age 87, range 72 to 98) were randomised. Those doing high-intensity resistance training increased muscle strength by 113% on average, versus 3% in non-exercisers, and walked faster. A nutritional supplement alone did not help. One trial, in nursing-home residents only.
source: Fiatarone et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 1994 (RCT, n=100)

text: How long should you hold a hamstring stretch? In a trial of 62 adults aged 65 to 97 with tight hamstrings, stretching five days a week for six weeks, 60-second holds gained range of motion faster than 30- or 15-second holds, and the gain lasted longer after stopping. The groups were small (13 to 17 people), and the authors note results may differ in younger adults.
source: Feland et al., Physical Therapy, 2001 (RCT, n=62)

text: A Cochrane review pooled 108 trials of exercise in people aged 60 and over living in the community. Exercise cut the rate of falls by 23%, and programmes built mainly on balance and functional exercises did about the same (24%). The authors rate these falls results high-certainty, but most trials had unclear or high risk of bias, and effects on things other than falls are less certain.
source: Sherrington et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2019 (108 RCTs, n=23,407)

text: A 2017 review of 18 randomised trials (3,824 older adults) found tai chi groups had fewer people falling and a lower rate of falls than control groups, and the benefit looked larger with more frequent practice. The authors caution that the effect may be overestimated because of publication bias and weaknesses in some of the original trials.
source: Huang et al., BMJ Open, 2017 (meta-analysis of 18 RCTs, n=3,824)

text: A 2022 meta-analysis of cohort studies found adults who did muscle-strengthening activities had about a 10-17% lower risk of death from any cause than those who did none. The biggest reduction came at roughly 30 to 60 minutes a week; beyond that the curve was J-shaped, and the authors say the effect of doing more is unclear. The data are observational and self-reported, and the authors rated the evidence very low quality.
source: Momma et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2022 (meta-analysis of cohort studies)

text: A study that followed 312 people aged 60 to 90 for a year found that those who fell had weaker big-toe and lesser-toe flexor muscles than those who did not. The authors suggest toe-strengthening may help — but the study only observed an association; it did not test whether training your toes or feet prevents falls.
source: Mickle et al., Clinical Biomechanics, 2009 (prospective cohort, n=312)
